To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
an increased level of chromosomal aberration (CA) in lymphocytes is associated with an increased risk of cancer.
the level of chromosomal aberration in lymphocytes is a relevant predictor of cancer risk.
an increased frequency of chromosome breaks in PBL is a relevant biomarker for the subsequent development of cancer in man.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the predictive value of biomarkers of genetic damage in relation to cancer risk.
the predictive value of biomarkers in human populations.
the identification of human biomarkers of exposure to environmental carcinogens.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
CA in PBL are predictive for cancer risk in man.
CA in PBL are predictive of subsequent cancer risk in humans.
there is no conclusive evidence that cytogenetic biomarkers in PBL are predictive for subsequent cancer risk in humans.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the predictive value of cytogenetic methods in PBL for subsequent cancer incidence is limited, but the data are encouraging and indicate that the use of such biomarkers should be pursued.
the predictive value of CA in PBL for subsequent cancer risk is supported by the results of our cohort study.
there is no evidence that PBL assays for CA, sister chromatid exchange, and micronuclei are predictive for cancer risk in the general population.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the level of CA in PBL is a good predictor of cancer risk.
the level of chromosome aberrations in PBL is predictive for the risk of cancer in a population of workers with a wide range of exposures to genotoxic agents.

chromosomal aberrations can serve as biomarkers for cancer risk, which is an important finding in the context of the current debate on the use of cytogenetic assays for the surveillance of the human population.
